title: Singapore pilots a government-built dating service
body: Singapore's government is trying its hand at matchmaking again. The country's Government Technology Agency (GovTech) has launched FirstDate , a pilot dating service for singles aged 21 to 35. For now, it's open only to public officers, according to the service's website. Applications close Oct. 5. FirstDate is designed as an alternative to endless swiping. Instead of browsing a stream of profiles, users fill out a questionnaire about their interests, habits, values, and preferences. The service then sends them one match per cycle (the time it takes to mutually accept and presumably meet up). Each match includes a compatibility score, a brief description of the person, and a personal note. SEE ALSO: The best hookup apps for 2026: I swiped until my thumb hurt The matching relies on the Gale-Shapley algorithm , a well-known mathematical method for pairing people based on their ranked preferences. It's the same approach used in some school admissions and medical residency matching systems. Most notably, the Match Group-owned Hinge also uses a version of it for its app and Hinge is the top dating app in Singapore , according to SimilarWeb, followed by Tinder and Bumble. Once matched, both people receive a text message and have 72 hours to accept the match. Contact details are exchanged only if both say yes. Couples who meet up can try "Date Quests," suggested activities meant to break the ice. Afterward, users get a short survey asking how things went, including whether they actually met in person. GovTech's site acknowledges that compatibility on paper doesn't guarantee chemist

title: NASA has a Dragon dilemma, and there appear to be no good answers
author: Eric Berger
body: For two decades, largely in service to the International Space Station, NASA has sought to foster an "economy" in low-Earth orbit. Twenty years ago, with a program to develop private spacecraft for cargo delivery to the space station, NASA sought to "stimulate efforts within the private sector to develop and operate safe, reliable, and cost-effective commercial space transportation systems." In recent years this has expanded to creating an entire commercial ecosystem in orbit, with transportation, space stations, manufacturing, tourism, and more, such that NASA is one of many customers in the market. In April 2024, the space agency explicitly laid out its philosophy: "NASA supports a robust commercial space economy that advances American industry and promotes technological discovery through in-space work and research. title: Here's what actually happened in OpenAI's Australian gov't server hack
author: Kyle Orland
body: Last week, when Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese told the world that an OpenAI agent had accessed "non-public files" from his country's Medicare statistics portal during testing, his description of the incident was a little light on details. Today, we're getting new information on just how far OpenAI's overzealous agent went in attempting to satisfy a rather innocuous-sounding informational prompt. In a newly published blog post , OpenAI says the June incident started when the company asked "an experimental, internal-only OpenAI model" to research government spending statistics in the Australian state of Victoria. When the model ran into trouble finding that data using the publicly published statistics that it was supposed to reference, "it took actions that we had not authorized it to take" to find an answer, OpenAI said. Those unauthorized actions included finding "a way to gain non-public access to the service" and using that access to view "technical system information and source code" alongside credentials and the aggregate statistics it was actually searching for, OpenAI said. title: Heres how to watch Andrew Scotts thirst-inducing performance in It Gets Worse
body: Earlier this September, Channel 4 released an NSFW clip from its upcoming comedy It Gets Worse that set the internet ablaze. SEE ALSO: NSFW clip of 'daddy' Andrew Scott has internet in a chokehold In the clip, series creator Leo Reich plays Ethan, an unsure 24-year-old who hooks up with a therapist ( Andrew Scott ). Scott's therapist tells Ethan "you're just a hole for daddy" before spitting in his mouth, reigniting every Fleabag viewer's Hot Priest thirst in the process. It Gets Worse is set to premiere on Channel 4 in the UK on Oct. 14, coinciding with its premiere at the BFI London Film Festival. American audiences will have to wait a bit longer to catch it, as It Gets Worse hits Paramount+ in early November. Produced by A24, the series follows three young people spiraling about their worsening adulthoods. In addition to Scott, it features a stacked list of guest stars, including Lena Dunham and Amelia Dimoldenberg. It Gets Worse is one of three British series from A24 that will call Paramount+ home, the streaming service announced today. The other two series are Major Players , an original drama about two girls hoping to start a women's soccer team, and The Ministry of Time , an adaptation of Kaliane Bradley s bestselling novel about a civil servant who must help a time-traveling Victorian-era polar explorer get used to the modern world. title: Spotify down: What we know so far
body: Updated on Tuesday, Sept. 29 at 12:40 p.m. ET Around 10:30 a.m. ET on Tuesday morning, Spotify confirmed that it was experiencing an outage. The company wrote on its X page: "We re aware of some issues right now and are checking them out!" This Tweet is currently unavailable. It might be loading or has been removed. No further information was available on the Spotify support site ; however, a notice reads, "The wait time to speak to an advisor is longer than usual." Meanwhile, DownDetector shows that user error reports for Spotify are still elevated but have been dropping steadily since around 12:15 p.m. ET. If Spotify won t play your morning playlist, you re far from alone. More than 15,000 people in the U.S. had reported problems with the streaming service by 10:06 a.m. ET on Tuesday, Sept. 29, according to DownDetector . The problems appear to vary. Some users can play music but can t search for songs or artists; others are seeing a "Something went wrong" message or having trouble logging in. Reports describe issues on both mobile and desktop, though the app may still work for some listeners. Credit: Screenshot/Spotify There s no confirmed cause or estimated time for a fix yet. If Spotify isn t working for you, trying its web player or another device may help, depending on which part of the service is affected. We ll update this story as more information becomes available.

title: Digger review: Tom Cruise swings big for Oscar gold, and dear God, does he miss
body: Tom Cruise has built his long and wildly successful career as an A-list movie star on his irrefutable charisma, incredible stunt-work capabilities, and a refusal to age. From early dramas like Top Gun, A Few Good Men, and Jerry Maguire , he defined the American hero, fighting the good fight in the face of death, failure, and a bellowing Jack Nicholson. Across Mission: Impossible movies, he created a brand that would define his legacy as an unstoppable force at the box office worldwide. But one honor he hasn't yet earned is an Academy Award. Make no mistake. He's been nominated for an acting Oscar three times twice for Best Actor ( Born on the Fourth of July, Jerry Maguire ) and once for Best Supporting Actor ( Magnolia). (That he was snubbed completely for Interview with the Vampire is an outrage that still echoes across the decades.) And while the Academy gave him an Honorary Award in 2026, Digger feels intensely as if it's Cruise's big swing to win at last. And I cannot imagine I rritu's latest will earn Cruise Oscar gold. On paper, it could. I rritu's Biutiful, Birdman, and The Revenant led to Academy Award nominations for Javier Bardem and Michael Keaton, and a win for Leonardo DiCaprio. However, his last film, Bardo: False Chronicle of a Handful of Truths , received less praise and only an Oscar nod for cinematography. And Digger, despite its energetic promotional campaign, has more in common with Bardo than Birdman in terms of the director's indulgences. Tom Cruise plays way against type in Digger . title: This study looks at how and with whom connected cars share your data
author: Jonathan M. Gitlin
body: In news that should surprise very few, connected cars remain a complete privacy nightmare. But now we have a better idea of what data those cars are giving away, and to whom, thanks to a study conducted by a team of researchers at Northeastern University and Consumer Reports . Testing 21 cars from 19 different brands revealed patterns of traffic to advertisers and trackers, as well as data shared with Big Tech firms like Microsoft and Adobe. And using a car’s companion app can multiply the problem, their testing found. In 2023, the Mozilla Foundation published a widely covered report looking at the privacy policies of more than two dozen automakers. They were appalled, writing that “cars are the worst product category we have ever reviewed for privacy.” But that analysis was conducted by sitting down and reading all the various privacy policies of each brand; today’s study involved measuring traffic from actual cars under a number of scenarios, including idling and being driven. The researchers even parked 11 cars—just the electric ones—in a Faraday tent to see if the loss of a cellular signal would push that traffic to the car’s Wi-Fi connection instead. Attempts to actually see what was in the data packets using modified certificates failed in every case. But “the network traces still yielded valuable information, including the domains contacted via DNS traffic, Server Name Indication (SNI) in TLS handshakes, the volume and timing of transmissions, and differences in behavior across experimental scenarios,” they found. title: Less protein for maggots means longer lives for fruit flies
author: Jacek Krywko
body: Back in the 1930s, scientists noticed that water fleas and rats fed restricted diets while young went on to live longer. The same effect has since turned up in fruit flies and mice. What we did not know was how a meal eaten in infancy could affect health weeks, months, or even years later. A recent Nature study might have found the answer. A team led by Fumiaki Obata, a biologist at the RIKEN Center for Biosystems Dynamics Research in Kobe, Japan, found a protein that carries a record into adulthood of what fruit flies ate as larvae, influencing how long they live. Hungry maggots Lab fruit flies are fed a mix of yeast and sugar, with yeast being their main source of protein. “We decreased only the yeast concentration in the diet, from eight percent to either one or two percent,” Obata explains. This low-protein diet was introduced roughly halfway through the larval period. Once the flies emerged from their pupae as adults, they returned to standard food. Read full article Comments

title: OpenAI says planned GPT-6.1 is too insecure to release
author: Kyle Orland
body: OpenAI says it has canceled plans to release its updated GPT-6.1 model next month as it continues to investigate what testing shows is a safety regression compared to previous models. The move, first reported by The Wall Street Journal late Monday and later confirmed in OpenAI statements to the press, reflects what OpenAI Head of Safety Systems Saachi Jain said was a "trade off" between performance and security seen when testing the now-scrapped model. Jain said GPT-6.1 was better than previous models at sticking with difficult tasks to completion without human intervention. But the model was also more likely to fail tests related to alignment (i.e. staying within the bounds set by human creators) and more willing to use sometimes "unsafe" tools and services to push ahead with a task. It was also more likely to try to deceive end users about actions it did or didn't take, Jain said. Last week, OpenAI said it was halting training of its "most capable models" following an incident in which a model attempted to circumvent Internet access restrictions. GPT-6.1 was not among those "most capable models" covered by that move, OpenAI told the WSJ. And while GPT-6.1 won't be released as is, the company said it intends to use the same base model for further training runs that it said will hopefully lead to future GPT-6 generation models. title: New Sonos Ace Ultra headphones have a genius linking feature I can’t live without
body: A decade ago, when my daughter was still very little, I had a genius idea: I was going to watch content on my TV, but I d use my headphones instead of speakers so I wouldn t wake the baby. The key, or so I thought, would be the ability to quickly switch from one to the other as needed, as watching an entire movie with headphones can be a little tiresome. As simple as that sounds, it didn t really work. My TV didn t support Bluetooth, and a wired connection required a very long cable that constantly got in the way. Later, TVs started getting Bluetooth, but connecting headphones always required an extra step, took a little too long, and the sound often lagged behind what was happening on screen. A few days ago, Sonos came up with a solution: The new Sonos Ace Ultra headphones can take over the audio from a compatible Sonos soundbar or speaker connected to the TV (in my case, Sonos provided a Sonos Beam Ultra soundbar). It's called headphone linking. Sonos Ace Ultra have a volume button that doubles as audio handover button. Credit: Stan Schroder/Mashable For the intricacies of that setup, and the performance of the headphones, I ll point you to our detailed review of the Sonos Ace Ultra . How Sonos headphone linking works Clicking and holding the volume button on the Sonos Ace Ultra headphones magically switches the audio from the soundbar to the headphones. And it wasn't just regular stereo; I immediately got the whole, immersive surround experience in the headphones, complete with head tracking so the sounds always came from the right spot. title: Seth Meyers takes A Closer Look at Trumps ballroom tour for Xi Jinping
body: Donald Trump 's two-day White House hosting of Chinese president Xi Jinping and his wife Peng Liyuan has dominated headlines and late night shows this week, and Seth Meyers took "A Closer Look." During Monday night's Late Night , the host used his deep dive segment to examine the presidential visit namely a state dinner at the White House, during which Trump invited attendees "through that beautiful curtain in the back" for a peek at the construction site that is Trump's controversial $400 million ballroom . "First of all, if someone invites you to go 'through that beautiful curtain in the back,' you need to get the out of there," said Meyers. "It's like the first scene in a horror movie that takes place in an antique store. Did you say you were looking for Hummel figurines? I believe I have some through the beautiful curtain in the back. Before we go, let me ask: Does anyone know you are here?" Notably, Trump previously told reporters the ballroom will sit atop an underground military complex "because of a stupid lawsuit that was filed," referring to the National Trust for Historic Preservation's seek to pause construction of the White House ballroom (U.S. District Court Judge Richard Leon ruled construction of the ballroom must sto p until the project is authorised by Congress, but work can continue for "the safety, security, and structural integrity of the White House.") " Isn't this ballroom of yours supposed to include a bunch of top secret military facilities, and if it does, maybe don't do the tour with the heads of foreign governments?" said Meyers on Late Night . body: Sonos' headphones have gone "Ultra," like the Bose QuietComfort Ultra before them. But what does that mean, exactly? Launched in 2024, the Sonos Ace were the company's first wireless, over-the-ear headphones . Now, the company has a new version, and the name itself Sonos Ace Ultra positions them above the old model and implies that these are really something special. Well, in a way, they are, but it really depends on how you plan on using them. I've spent a week with the Sonos Ace Ultra headphones to see how they compare to the noise-cancelling competition , and I enjoyed the comfort, the surround sound, and the fact that they're connected to the Sonos speaker system in my house. For pure music listening, though, they're just OK. Design: Mostly unchanged The Sonos Ace Ultra looks pretty much the same as the old model. It's an understated look that's typical of Sonos gadgets, and you do get two new colors on offer: Sand and Agave (besides the old Soft White and Black). The unit Sonos sent me was in the Agave color, and I love it; it's a very subtle shade of green-blue that goes well with anything. What is this, a cable for ants? Credit: Stan Schroeder/Mashable Don't expect anything flashy. The Sonos Ace Ultra looks like a nice set of headphones, nothing more and nothing less. Apple's AirPods Max 2 have a shinier, more recognizable look, despite also being available in very subtle colors. title: Experts worry about Nvidia's AI chip sales in China and influence over Trump
author: Ashley Belanger
body: On its face, the recent summit between Donald Trump and China’s president Xi Jinping didn’t change much in the world of AI regulation. Export controls were not discussed, with neither country seemingly interested in making concessions. An already tenuous trade truce was temporarily extended for just two months, and looming US controls that could drop soon could easily end that and trigger China to retaliate by cutting off exports of rare earths, analysts expect. However, in the background of these shaky talks, Nvidia appeared to notch a big win, as China is currently mulling relaxing controls and allowing some of its biggest AI firms to import perhaps millions more of Nvidia’s banned chips over the next year. Sources familiar with China’s talks told The Information that China’s tech oversight arm, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, asked Alibaba and ByteDance to share plans to buy Nvidia’s RTX Pro 5500 chips. Although these are gaming chips, China asked firms to detail how they plan to use them, with expectations that chips could be put into servers to help power the country’s most in-demand AI models. title: SpaceX's Starship goes orbital, deploying first next-gen Starlinks
author: Stephen Clark
body: SpaceX's Starship rocket thundered into the sky over South Texas early Monday. It was the 14th test flight of the world's most powerful launch vehicle. This time, however, the rocket's massive upper stage squeezed out some extra oomph from its Raptor engines and accelerated to orbital velocity. On all of Starship's previous flights, SpaceX intentionally dialed back the full capability of the rocket to fly a suborbital trajectory, slow enough for Earth's gravity to pull the vehicle back into the atmosphere before it could complete a full lap around the planet. After several successful suborbital flights in a row, SpaceX officials decided this launch should go all the way to low-Earth orbit. And it did. What's more, SpaceX packed 26 of the company's newest generation of Starlink broadband satellites into the rocket's cargo bay. One by one, the flat-packed satellites —too large to fit inside SpaceX's workhorse Falcon 9 rocket —were released from Starship's payload deployer using a system of pulleys and cables to eject the satellites overboard like a Pez dispenser spits out candy. title: Florida invokes extinction fears in legal bid to halt OpenAI development
author: Kyle Orland
body: The state of Florida is seeking a temporary injunction to stop OpenAI from continuing to develop what it calls a "reckless, unacceptably risky product" without the deployment of "third-party approved safety guardrails." The new legal motion , filed Monday morning, is part of a civil lawsuit the state of Florida originally filed in June, arguing that ChatGPT represented "a threat to the public safety of Floridians," specifically by preying on vulnerable populations like children and violent or delusional adults. But that original lawsuit came before the Hugging Face hacking incident and the subsequent publicized warnings of catastrophic misalignment risk that have spurred industry-wide calls to slow the development and training of so-called frontier models. Following that string of events, OpenAI on Friday announced it had already halted training of its "most-capable models" until it could validate safety protocols intended to prevent agents from accessing the open Internet during training. But in seeking an injunction from the state court, Florida argues that OpenAI has "repeatedly shown they are incapable of monitoring their AI, and hesitant in revealing rogue activity once discovered." title: New device captures carbon dioxide by pumping it across a battery
author: Scott K. Johnson
body: Equipment to capture carbon dioxide from ambient air or smokestacks generally works through a sort of reversible filter. Air is passed through granules or a liquid that absorbs the CO 2 , then that CO 2 -loaded substance undergoes a process (usually heating) that causes it to let go of all that CO 2 . The resulting gas can be collected in a separated stream. It’s also possible to do a similar sort of operation on a smaller scale—like inside a battery. A new study from a team led by James Buchen of the University of Delaware demonstrates an example of a battery-based electrochemical carbon-capture technique that they say is more viable than previous attempts. It has the potential to require less energy—and therefore be cheaper—than the reversible-filter designs that currently dominate. Carbon chemistry The basic idea behind a device of this type is that hydroxide produced at the battery cathode reacts with CO 2 , converting it to carbonate or bicarbonate that passes through the separator membrane to the anode. There, the lower pH causes the reaction to reverse, with carbonate turning back into CO 2 gas. The role of the cathode is to produce hydroxide ions; the role of the anode is to consume them. title: To keep drug prices high, pharma has been piling up the patents
author: Beth Mole
body: The cost of healthcare in general is a debilitating, pre-existing condition for Americans. But the high prices of prescription drugs usually stand out as a pain point. While there are many insidious reasons why Americans pay more—often far more—for their medicines than people in peer countries, exploitation of the US patent system is an obvious one. A study published Monday in JAMA highlights just how much patent exploitation has grown since 1990. In that time, researchers found the number of patents on small-molecule drugs have more than tripled, going from an average of 2.1 patents per drug approved in 1990 to 6.9 for those approved in 2019. Most of the growth was in "nonprimary" patents—patents that generally aren't related to a drug's active ingredient, but are instead for things like minor tweaks to a drug's non-active ingredients, updates to the way the drug is used, or the design of specialty delivery devices, such as auto-injectors. Together, those extra patents on an individual drug can create what's called a "patent thicket," which delays the release of affordable generics on the market, keeping drug prices higher for longer without actual clinical advancements. title: Trump cuts fuel economy standards back to 2014 levels
author: Jonathan M. Gitlin
body: The federal government’s war on fuel efficiency claimed another victim today. The Department of Transportation released a new rule for the country’s Corporate Average Fuel Economy standards, which, as expected, discourage the very idea of economical vehicles. Among the changes is a rollback to fuel economy numbers not seen in more than a decade, below even the low standards implemented in 2020 , the last time President Trump was in power. The new goal is just 34.9 mpg by model year 2031. This is nothing if not expected. When Sean Duffy was installed as Transportation secretary last January, he immediately announced that any fuel efficiency standards put in place under the Biden administration were dead and buried. Those rules had a slower ramp up than some might have liked but would have required automakers to sell many more electric vehicles and plug-in hybrids. Now, we may have the possibility of some OEMs dropping their EVs and PHEVs entirely. The notice of final rulemaking criticizes the idea of emissions credits and blames them for automakers not investing in cleaner engine technology, and from model year 2028, such credits are a thing of the past. And plug-in vehicles will now no longer be included in an automaker’s fleet average; under previous rules an EV or PHEV could have a CAFE rating of hundreds of mpg . Read full article Comments

title: Kalshi loses again as judges rule prediction markets must obey gambling laws
author: Jon Brodkin
body: Another federal appeals court has ruled that states can enforce their gambling laws against the prediction market Kalshi, which asserts that it can only be regulated by the US government. On Friday, a three-judge panel in the US Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit ruled unanimously against Kalshi and in favor of Ohio and Tennessee. While the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission has exclusive jurisdiction over "swaps," the judges found that sports wagers offered on Kalshi do not meet the legal definition of swaps. Moreover, the court found that even if Kalshi wagers were swaps, the regulatory scheme created by Congress would not prohibit states from enforcing gambling laws on prediction markets. "We hold that Kalshi has not shown that its sports-event contracts satisfy the statutory definition of a 'swap' so as to fall within the scope of the CFTC's 'exclusive jurisdiction,'" said the ruling written by Judge Julia Smith Gibbons, a George W. Bush appointee. "And, even assuming that Kalshi’s sports-event contracts are swaps, we alternatively hold that the CEA [Commodity Exchange Act] neither expressly nor impliedly preempts Ohio’s or Tennessee’s gambling laws." title: Scientists solve 1840s space weather mystery
author: Jennifer Ouellette
body: The infamous Carrington Event of 1859 has long been considered the first extreme space weather event, but there have been reports of minor disturbances to telegraph equipment during geomagnetic storms since the late 1840s. In 2013, scholars discovered an anonymous report published in 1871 in Nature describing how a "very intense magnetic disturbance" disrupted rail travel in Exeter on the southern coast of England in October 1841. If accurate, this would be the earliest such account. However, according to a paper published in the journal Space Weather, that 1841 date is most likely a typo, with the real railway disruption occurring several years later. "Space weather is often discussed as a modern challenge because of our dependence on technologies such as satellites, communications systems and electricity networks," said co-author Jim Wild of Lancaster University. "What this study shows is that society has been experiencing the effects of space weather on technology for almost as long as electrical technologies have existed. The Exeter train delay is a fascinating story because it sits right at the point where emerging technologies first began to encounter the realities of the space environment." The Carrington Event remains the most powerful geomagnetic storm in the scientific record, with strong auroral displays occurring all over the world, causing sparking and even a few fires in telegraph stations. title: F1 in Azerbaijan: That was almost a close-run thing
author: Jonathan M. Gitlin
body: Formula 1 raced on the streets of Baku, Azerbaijan, this past weekend. Although the race predates Liberty’s acquisition of the sport by a few months , it’s a rather good microcosm of the sport as it exists today. The track is a real challenge; it takes place on dusty city streets lined with concrete walls and through a medieval fortress gate, followed by a 1.4-mile (2.2 km) flat-out blast to the finish line, with gusts of wind from the Caspian Sea a block away. It’s interesting to look at Baku’s mix of modern and classical architecture sharing the stage with a massive hospitality and pit lane complex. And since it wouldn’t be F1 without some controversy, this year the race was held a day earlier than normal after F1 switched up its schedule to avoid clashing with Azerbaijan’s celebration of its recent war with Armenia—it’s almost as if Bernie Ecclestone had never left. The proximity of the walls leaves very little margin for error at the speeds F1 cars go around Baku. Last year , qualifying was interrupted by no less than six red flags after crashes. title: OpenAI halts frontier-model training amid string of agent misalignment incidents
author: Kyle Orland
body: OpenAI says it has paused all internal training of "our most capable models" as it continues what CEO Sam Altman is calling "an extensive and ongoing review related to our agents’ use of internet access during training and evaluation." The company revealed the pause in a report about a so-called misalignment incident in which an agent attempted to exploit a gap in Internet-access restrictions during a routine research task during training. OpenAI says that improper DNS filtering allowed the agent to attempt to break out of its sandbox and access the wider Internet when asked for biographical details about a blogger. OpenAI says the agent was only able to access the company's offline web cache and that it has implemented additional multi-layered blocking controls to prevent similar incidents in the future. Despite that, though, the company says it has decided to "pause all other training, evaluation, and inference with tool-use" for this frontier model "until we have both validated that the gap is resolved and performed additional red-teaming of the system." title: Modders discover way to play PS5 games on Xbox consoles
body: If you've ever had a lingering curiosity wondering if PlayStation games can be played on an Xbox , well, they can. Technically. A modder named Devran Cosmo Uenal has built an early version of a PS5 emulator for the Xbox Series X, according to Boy Genius Report . The project, called PS5X, can already run a small selection of PS5 games on Microsoft's console, though not especially smoothly. For context, an emulator is software that imitates another device's hardware. Consoles are essentially specialized computers, and their games are built to run on that specific hardware. An emulator tricks a game into thinking it's running on the machine it was made for, even when it's actually on a PC, a phone, or, in this case, a rival console. Emulation sits in murky legal territory. In the U.S., emulators themselves are generally legal because building software that emulates a console's hardware isn't illegal in itself. However, downloading copies of a video game you don't own is copyright infringement. PS5X is a port of KytyPS5, an open-source PS5 emulator for PC. Uenal adapted it to run on the Xbox Series X. BGR reports that the Xbox version lags behind the PC original but already produces impressive results for such an early project. SEE ALSO: Xbox lays off more than 250 employees amid studio restructurings Early is the keyword here, as the list of games PS5X can play is very short. title: Starship reaches orbit for the first time ever but returns home early
body: UPDATE: Sep. 28, 2026, 11:46 a.m. EDT Starship splashed down in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of Hawaii at about 11 a.m. CT on Monday, Sept. 28, 2026. SpaceX officials have not yet said why controllers decided to bring the ship home early after a successful orbital insertion maneuver, a first for Starship. The test was supposed to last about 10 hours to see the ship complete six full orbits around Earth. Instead, the mission ran just three hours. SpaceX 's Starship reached orbit for the first time on Monday, surviving an early engine shutdown during ascent, before flight controllers opted to cut the test flight short. The giant rocket lifted off at 7:48 a.m. local time from Starbase, Texas . Moments later, one of the six engines on Starship's upper stage, known as the ship, quit firing. At first, SpaceX seemed to be leaning toward calling off the push to orbit, with host Dan Huot providing live commentary as the team weighed the decision. But after studying the data, controllers polled "go" for the orbital insertion engine burn. A single engine fired for a few seconds and pushed the ship fast enough to stay in space . "That's the first time we've ever said that in this program: 'Go for orbit,'" said Jake Berkowitz, a SpaceX lead propulsion engineer. "That is a really, really cool thing to hear and obviously means quite a bit for the remainder of this mission." Reaching orbit moves Starship toward sustained spaceflight. title: Microsoft goes quiet after church groups ask for 1% of data center costs
author: Ashley Belanger
body: Microsoft has spent all year telling communities that when it brings a new data center into their area, it is committed to being a “good neighbor." It will pay local property taxes that support local hospitals, schools, parks, and libraries, and it will invest in “vital services the community cares about,” the company promised. And it has sent liaisons into those communities to learn what those needs are. But ask those liaisons how much the company is willing to invest, and the answers can be hard to come by. At community meetings, Microsoft representatives have seemed unprepared to answer questions that go beyond the company's “good neighbor” campaign materials, Ars has learned. The company has acknowledged in public-facing documents that simply matching its employees’ charitable donations—which totaled $229 million across 29,000 nonprofits in 2024—isn't enough. But it has been vague about what more substantial local investments might look like. And to critics, Microsoft’s local investments seem especially small compared with the estimated hundreds of millions in state-level tax breaks that data center developers get in 38 states—exemptions that often last more than a decade. The first round sees you trying to guess the word, with correct, misplaced, and incorrect letters shown in each guess. title: Moon phase today: What the Moon will look like on September 28, 2026
body: The Full Moon has passed, but the Moon will still look almost completely lit tonight. It's now beginning to wane, although you probably won't notice much difference from the night before. Here's what you can spot on the lunar surface tonight. What is today s Moon phase? As of Monday, Sept. 28, NASA's Daily Moon Guide tracker tells us the Moon is in the Waning Gibbous phase, with 97% of its surface visible. There's still so much to see tonight, including the Mare Imbrium, Mare Serenitatis, and Mare Tranquillitatis which can be spotted without visual aids. If you have binoculars, they'll also help you see the Clavius Crater, the Alphonsus Crater, and the Gassendi Crater. Finally, if you have access to a telescope, you'll see the Apollo 12 and 16 landing spots, plus the Rima Caucasus Mountains. When is the next Full Moon? The next Full Moon will take place on October 25 or 26, depending on your timezone. What are Moon phases? The Moon goes through a repeating cycle as it orbits Earth, taking roughly 29.5 days to complete. During that time, the amount of its sunlit side visible from Earth changes, giving us the different lunar phases. It starts with a slim crescent, grows to a half Moon and eventually reaches the Full Moon, before beginning the cycle again. NASA explains that which phase we see depends on where the Moon is in relation to Earth and the Sun. The eight phases are: New Moon - The Moon is between Earth and the sun, so the side we see is dark (in other words, it's invisible to the eye). title: A Long Winter review: Fred Hechinger fronts a beautiful, unmissable queer drama
body: There's a unique heartbreak to realizing our parents aren't who we imagined. A Long Winter is about that agony, and how one might grow from it. From English writer/director Andrew Haigh ( Weekend, All of Us Strangers ) A Long Winter centers on a quietly queer protagonist, who comes to understand himself and what he wants through the hard, cold lesson of who his parents really are. And the result is elegant in its heartbreak. SEE ALSO: TIFF 2026 preview: 18 films (and shows) you'll want to see (and how) What is A Long Winter About? Fred Hechinger and Ebon Moss-Bachrach in "A Long Winter." Credit: TIFF Adapted from Colm T ib n's short story of the same name, A Long Winter is set in the brutally cold mountains of Colorado, during the early 1950s. There, despite the hard work of maintaining the house and farm animals, Mike ( Fear Street ' s Fred Hechinger) enjoys a rather blissful existence, relishing the time with his younger brother ( Heartstopper 's Kit Connor ), his mother ( Outlander 's Caitr ona Balfe), and father ( The Bear 's Ebon Moss-Bachrach ). However, once his brother takes a job far away, Mike witnesses another side of his parents, one tarnished by regret and recrimination. As another winter approaches, his mother Louise's smiles turn to snarls. Her empty water glass reeks of alcohol, and her fury at her hard-headed husband Lester boils over. One day, she wanders off with their dog, Sandy. Hours later, a blizzard turns the familiar hills to treacherous, frigid white. Where did she go? Could she have survived? body: Welcome to your guide to Pips, the latest game in the New York Times catalog. Released in August 2025, Pips puts a unique spin on dominoes, creating a fun single-player experience that could become your next daily gaming habit. How to play Pips If you've ever played dominoes, you'll have a passing familiarity with how Pips is played. As we've shared in our previous hints stories for Pips, the tiles, like dominoes, are placed vertically or horizontally and connect with each other. The main difference between a traditional game of dominoes and Pips is the color-coded conditions you have to address. The touching tiles don't necessarily have to match. SEE ALSO: Wordle today: Answer, hints for September 28, 2026 The conditions you have to meet are specific to the color-coded spaces. For example, if it provides a single number, every side of a tile in that space must add up to the number provided. It is possible and common for only half a tile to be within a color-coded space. title: Instagram’s new Pixel effect takes the relationship soft launch to another level
body: First came the hand across the dinner table. Then the second drink, the carefully cropped shoulder, and the suspiciously tall shadow. Now Instagram has a new way to hint that you re seeing someone. The platform s new Pixel effect lets you blur a person or object in a Story by describing what you want pixelated in a text prompt. In a post showing off the effect , Instagram leaned into its dating potential: "Soft launching? We got you." If you re unfamiliar with the ritual, a soft launch lets your followers know there s a new person in your life without telling them exactly who it is. You might post their hand or the back of their head. Pixel takes that idea a step further: Everyone can see that your date is in the photo, but their identity remains a mystery. And there s an audience for that kind of reveal. Tinder data reported by Mashable in 2023 found that 26 percent of UK 18- to 34-year-olds would rather gradually reveal a new partner online, compared with 8 percent who preferred a big announcement. In a recent Tinder survey , 46 percent of single Gen Z social media users in the U.S. said they soft-launch relationships, while 37 percent said they hard-launch them. title: Samsung smart fridges stop cooling after faulty update
body: A refrigerator has one job you really don t want interrupted by a software update. For some Samsung owners in South Korea, though, an update left their fridges unable to keep food cold. The trouble began Sept. 22, when customers installed refrigerator software through Samsung s SmartThings app. Owners reported dark interior lights, screens stuck on an "updating" message, and fridges that had stopped cooling. The affected models were reportedly mostly Bespoke AI four-door refrigerators released since 2024. SEE ALSO: Apple's iPhone Duo is here, and Samsung is already throwing shade The timing made a bad situation worse. Chuseok, a major Korean holiday centered on family gatherings and food, was about to begin. One owner told Seoul Shinmun they had thrown away 20 kilograms of food; others worried about meat and other groceries they had bought for the holiday. Samsung acknowledged the problem on its community forum, saying an error during software testing had caused power and screen problems for some customers. According to South Korean reporting , software meant for internal testing was mistakenly sent to customers. Samsung stopped distributing it, offered free repairs, and aimed to restore affected refrigerators by Sept. 24. The company said it was still reviewing compensation for spoiled food. It has not publicly confirmed how many fridges were affected or whether every repair was completed by that target date. The outage raises a question that goes well beyond Samsung. title: How the Smithsonian became the latest front in Trump’s culture war
author: Alec MacGillis, ProPublica
body: In November 2021, the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History opened an exhibit called “The Electric Dr. Franklin,” describing “Benjamin Franklin’s pioneering contributions to electrical science.” The exhibit explained that, prior to becoming an abolitionist, he had enslaved people in his household. “Benjamin Franklin’s remarkable scientific accomplishments were, in part, enabled by slavery,” it declared. The exhibit speculated that Franklin may have used enslaved people in his electrical research. “Franklin wrote about experiments in which he took shocks and used family and friends in these ways, although he seldom identified who in particular assisted him,” stated the exhibit, which closed in 2025 but can still be found online . “Indentured servants and enslaved people in his household could also have been used, although we may never know for certain.” It was an eye-catching conjecture: one of the most revered of the Founding Fathers subjecting people held against their will to possibly painful shocks. And it was one of many details singled out for criticism in a blistering 162-page White House report released in July that argued that the museum had fallen victim to an “ideological capture” that “moved the Museum’s mission away from straightforward historical education and scholarship toward an extreme political activism that seeks to transform our country.” Read full article Comments

title: Can SpaceXs Starship actually loop Earth six times? Watch it live.
body: After more than 40 months of test flights, SpaceX will attempt to put its mammoth Starship into orbit around Earth for the first time and bring it back for a safe landing 10 hours later. The company, founded by billionaire Elon Musk , plans to launch the rocket from its private pad in Starbase, Texas , as early as 8:15 a.m. ET on Monday, Sept. 28. Prior flights that have reached space have only flown straight up and down, meaning gravity has naturally pulled Starship back toward the ground like a tossed ball. But to stay in space, it must instead fly sideways at 17,500 mph. At that staggering speed, the spacecraft is still "falling" toward the ground, but Earth's surface is curving away at the exact same rate. That's what allows the spacecraft to continuously stay in space without ever crashing back to the planet. "Flight tests until this point have intentionally flown passively safe suborbital trajectories to maximize public safety while allowing for maximum learning," according to SpaceX . "By going to orbit, the next phase of developing Starship to be fully and rapidly reusable can begin." The upcoming test, marking Starship's 14th flight, is the latest step in the company's long campaign to turn the most powerful rocket ever built into a reusable vehicle one that can haul heavy cargo, survive a scorching plunge back to Earth, and support NASA 's Artemis moon missions. Beyond that, Musk's personal priority is to use the rocket and ship to send people to Mars. title: Wild Horse Nine review: Is John Malkovich at the center of a meta puzzle?
body: As a comedy, Wild Horse Nine works fine. British-Irish playwright-turned-filmmaker Martin McDonagh imbues it with the blisteringly macabre sense of humor that he's forged in work like his 2003 play The Pillowman and his feature film debut In Bruges, as well as later movies like Seven Psychopaths; Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri ; and The Banshees of Inisherin . As a Martin McDonagh comedy, it feels a bit redundant. But perhaps that's precisely the point? From its premise, Wild Horse Nine echoes the plot of McDonagh's first feature film, In Bruges. Both films center on a pair of contract killers who have an uneasy friendship, and who travel to a lovely vacation spot with a potentially deadly outcome looming over them. This time, McDonagh has cast John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell in the roles of CIA agents who are chaotically compelling and lethally reckless. Within these roles, Malkovich and Rockwell are invited to repeat themselves, creating echoes that actually bolsters the film's message about the mind-bending nature of looking back. Wild Horse Nine is an oddball's elegy. title: Moon phase today: What the Moon will look like on September 27, 2026
body: The Full Moon has now passed, but it won't disappear from view quite yet. The Moon will still look almost completely illuminated tonight as it begins to wane, with only a small difference from yesterday. What is today s Moon phase? As of Sunday, Sept. 27, NASA's Daily Moon Guide tracker tells us the Moon is in the Waning Gibbous phase, with 99% of its surface visible. There's still so much to see tonight, including the Mare Imbrium, Mare Vaporum, and Kepler Crater which can be spotted without visual aids. If you have binoculars, they'll also help you see the Clavius Crater, the Alphonsus Crater, and the Archimedes Crater. Finally, if you have access to a telescope, you'll see the Apollo 14 and 15 landing spots, and the Rima Ariadaeus. When is the next Full Moon? The next Full Moon will take place on October 25 or 26, depending on your timezone. What are Moon phases? The Moon goes through a repeating cycle as it orbits Earth, taking roughly 29.5 days to complete. During that time, the amount of its sunlit side visible from Earth changes, giving us the different lunar phases. It starts with a slim crescent, grows to a half Moon and eventually reaches the Full Moon, before beginning the cycle again. NASA explains that which phase we see depends on where the Moon is in relation to Earth and the Sun. The eight phases are: New Moon - The Moon is between Earth and the sun, so the side we see is dark (in other words, it's invisible to the eye). title: Appeals court says Ohio and Tennessee can regulate Kalshi under gambling laws
body: Kalshi lost another round Friday in its fight over whether states can treat prediction markets as gambling. A three-judge panel of the 6th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in Cincinnati ruled that Ohio and Tennessee can apply their gambling laws to Kalshi's event contracts, Reuters reported . Kalshi's central argument is that its sports contracts are "swaps," financial products that fall under the CFTC's exclusive oversight rather than state gambling rules. The court rejected that. SEE ALSO: Polymarket and Kalshi face possible regulation as Supreme Court 'monitors the situation' Writing for the panel, Circuit Judge Julia Smith Gibbons said swaps generally refer to financial instruments used to hedge risk, not gaming-related contracts. She added that regulating gambling is a core part of a state's police power, and that the federal Commodity Exchange Act does not override Ohio's or Tennessee's gambling laws, according to Reuters. Gibbons also questioned how betting on the number of corner kicks in a soccer match, or on a long-shot parlay, serves the federal law's goal of helping people manage financial risk. The ruling overturned a preliminary injunction that had barred Tennessee from enforcing its gambling laws against Kalshi. It also upheld a lower court's refusal to grant Kalshi a similar injunction in Ohio. Tennessee Attorney General Jonathan Skrmetti called the decision a "great win" for the state. title: Werwulf trailer: Willem Dafoe hunts Aaron Taylor-Johnson in Robert Eggers latest
body: What do you want for Christmas? If your answer sounded anything like, "to get spooked by a new Robert Eggers film," you're in luck! The director's new film Werwulf hits theaters this December, and based on the latest trailer, it's going to be an unnerving ride. Co-written by Eggers ( Nosferatu ) and his The Northman collaborator Sj n, Werwulf transports viewers to a village in 13th-century England that's been weathering mysterious attacks from a great beast. Little do the villagers know that the beast may lurk among them, disguised in human form. That beast is none other than a local farmer (Aaron Taylor-Johnson) who's been cursed with a horrifying case of lycanthropy. In the trailer above, a disembodied voice commands the farmer to "feed upon the flesh of mankind, and I will give thee back thy soul," suggesting that the werewolf's attacks are a twist form of self-preservation. The farmer's time may soon be up, as a skilled hunter ( Willem Dafoe ) soon turns up in the village to exterminate the wolf. While the farmer's wife (Lily-Rose Depp) insists that her husband is a good man, will that be enough to save him? Check out the full trailer above to get a frightening preview of what's to come, and feast your eyes on Eggers' trademark attention to period details. Just don't expect any footage of Taylor-Johnson in his wolf form. Some things might just have to wait until release. Werwulf hits theaters Dec. 25.

The Harvest Moon is the Full Moon closest to the September equinox, which falls around the start of autumn in the Northern Hemisphere. This year, September's Full Moon comes just a few days after the equinox. September's Full Moon is also known as the Corn Moon, a name linked to the time of year when crops are gathered, according to Royal Museums Greenwich . When is the next full moon? title: Microsoft is ending support for Internet Explorer mode in Edge
body: Internet Explorer's last foothold on modern Windows now has an expiration date. Microsoft is reminding IT administrators that Internet Explorer mode in its Edge browser, the only remaining way to run IE's rendering engine on current versions of Windows, will be supported through at least the end of 2029, according to gHacks Tech News . The notice, posted in the Microsoft 365 admin center under message ID MC1473151, tells organizations that still depend on IE-only applications to start planning their migrations now. SEE ALSO: Microsoft's new Surface laptops get rid of Copilot+ PC branding According to gHacks, the company has committed to announcing an end-of-support date at least a year before it takes effect. The early warning is to give admins time to rebuild or replace internal software, which can take years. For context, IE mode is a compatibility feature inside Edge. Edge is built on Google's open-source Chromium engine, but IE mode lets it load pages with Trident, the older engine that powered Internet Explorer 11. Microsoft first flagged the mode's eventual retirement in 2021, according to gHacks. Organizations with no IE dependencies don't need to take any action. For companies that still depend on it, Microsoft's guidance is to identify what depends on IE mode and update or replace it. The notice is the latest step in a long wind-down. Microsoft officially retired the standalone Internet Explorer 11 browser in June 2022 , 26 years after the browser shipped with early versions of Windows. At that point, Microsoft began steering anyone who tried to open IE toward Edge

title: Social media platforms refuse to run paid ads for Musk documentary
body: Musk , Alex Gibney's four-hour documentary about Elon Musk , hits theaters in two weeks and received rave reviews out of its premiere at the Venice International Film Festival. Yet distributor Bleecker Street can't buy ads on major social media platforms in order to promote it. SEE ALSO: 'Musk' documentary trailer is finally here According to The Hollywood Reporter , YouTube , TikTok , and Meta , which owns Instagram and Facebook , have all refused to run the trailer for Musk . The same goes for X, which is owned by Musk and which reportedly won't accept advertising for Bleecker Street's other upcoming releases. YouTube, TikTok, and Meta told Bleecker Street representatives that they rejected the trailer because of "political content." TikTok and Meta do not allow paid political and campaign ads, with Meta's rules stemming from the Cambridge Analytica scandal. YouTube does, with ads requiring "paid for" disclosures. The Musk trailer contains references to the 2024 election, but it is not itself a political campaign. Bleecker Street has appealed YouTube, TikTok, and Meta's decision. While YouTube and TikTok are still mulling over the request, Meta has rejected it outright. This isn't the first bump in the road for Musk . Universal Pictures, which is distributing the film internationally, reportedly got cold feet on releasing Musk . Cloudflare sits between websites and all those agents, and allows website owners some level of control: Owners can block all those AI tools, allow them, or, as you’ll hear, only allow those that might pay money for access. title: Tesla’s big electric truck faces an even bigger infrastructure challenge
author: Aarian Marshall, wired.com
body: Tesla CEO Elon Musk has insisted investors think of his electric automaker as a robotics and autonomous vehicle company now. He’s targeted a $20 trillion valuation—nearly four times the value of market leader Nvidia —on that premise. But his Tesla team was in Sparks, Nevada, on Thursday to focus on, well, an electric vehicle: the long-awaited Tesla Semi . The Semi concept first rolled onto a Tesla event stage in late 2017 . Nearly a decade later, Tesla officially launched high-volume production at a livestreamed but invite-only event at the company’s factory. It targeted a niche audience: the cost-conscious people who manage large trucking fleets. A handful of them, all men, trooped across the stage to be thanked for their orders to a pulsing techno beat. “It’s going to be, really, a driver’s truck. It’s like a sports car in truck form.” Musk said in a pre-taped video played during the evening event. (Musk, for years the ringmaster at Tesla’s circus-like events, skipped his second vehicle debut in a row ; he was attending a White House China State Dinner featuring President Xi Jinping .) title: Liftoff: Google is realizing Elon Musks dream of AI data centers in space
body: Next week, Google will be living out Elon Musk's dream of putting AI data centers in space and they'll be doing it with help from Musk's space exploration company. On Thursday, October 1, 2026, Google will load an experimental satellite on SpaceX's Falcon 9 rocket and launch it in space. The satellite is part of Google's Project Suncatcher initiative, which seeks to set up AI data centers in space. The experimental satellite will be able answer simple A.I. prompts from space, according to the New York Times . In a blog post about Project Suncatcher , Google explained the potential benefits of sending data centers into orbit: Cooling orbital data centers is a crucial research challenge. TPUs generate a large amount of heat in a small area, which needs to be diffused safely or the chips are at risk of overheating. But in space, there s no airflow. In a vacuum, you can only diffuse heat via radiators, which requires a totally different approach to cooling electronics. As the New York Times reported, Google isn't sending a full-on orbital data center this time; it's sending the potential precursor to one. The satellite, named MVP, contains four tensor processing units, which are specialized chips with the computing power of one server in a data center here on Earth. The computer chips will be powered by the satellite's solar panels, which will provide one kilowatt of power to the chips. title: A Mars crater wasnt just a lake. That could change the hunt for life.
body: A Martian rock formation that looked like an ancient shoreline from space now appears to preserve a much more astonishing water history. Since 2021, NASA 's Perseverance rover has explored Jezero crater, a 28-mile-wide basin on Mars where rivers once fed a lake. Scientists had hoped to find sedimentary rocks along the crater's edge a clue that would support the lakeshore prediction. But, in a twist, the rover discovered these rocks are igneous, meaning their origins are volcanic and not formed by the lake. Water, the rover found, had actually soaked the rocks at least three separate times, in three different ways. This new understanding of the Jezero landmark, dubbed the "margin unit," gives scientists a fuller picture of ancient Mars, revealing a planet where water kept finding new ways to move through the landscape. Though the rover data didn't reveal evidence of life, they did show an abundance of carbonates minerals known to be good at locking in traces of past microbes . On Earth, these minerals often form in shallow oceans and lakes that host life. "Jezero Crater sits inside one of the largest exposures of carbonate on Mars," said Candice Bedford, a scientist at Purdue University in Indiana, in a statement . "What we learn here reaches well beyond this crater." title: AI leaders say they want safety, but on whose terms?
body: As anxiety mounts over artificial intelligence safety, a number of leaders who helm frontier labs have made clear that they want and need better industry standards to contain the potentially dangerous technology . Yet, like any industry leader hoping to achieve the most favorable conditions for their companies, AI executives like Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, and Google DeepMind co-founder Demis Hassabis are hoping to play a significant role in determining the standards they seek, say experts. SEE ALSO: AI drift: The catastrophic risk you're taking but don't realize "I think what has happened recently is that they've fully come to terms with the fact that they actually can't keep these things safe," Anthony Aguirre, CEO and president of the Future of Life Institute told Mashable. The nonprofit organization focuses on preventing extreme large-scale risks of transformative technologies. Yet, Aguirre added, the fresh candor comes with a catch: "Certainly they want to be in control of the process." What that could look like for leading AI companies is self-regulation, along with transparency and accountability on their terms, plus assurances about antitrust law. AI companies want artificial general intelligence Aguirre said that despite recognizing perilous emergent safety concerns, major AI companies still won't abandon their goal of achieving artificial general intelligence, or AGI. This form of AI would match or exceed human intelligence, and it could lead to the replacement of many human jobs with automated ones along with the rise of AI decision makers

title: Paper Tiger review: Adam Driver, Miles Teller, and Scarlett Johansson enter a tense love triangle
body: Marriage Story stars Adam Driver and Scarlett Johansson reunite in writer/director James Gray's Paper Tiger. But don't expect a desperate rehash of Noah Baumbach's divorce drama. For one thing, Gray is a filmmaker less drawn to such wall-punching theatrics, as evident through films like Two Lovers, Ad Astra, and Armageddon Time . For another, Driver and Johansson are not lovers in this film, though they are in a love triangle of sorts, with Miles Teller at the center. Gray gives Driver, Johansson, and Teller some unexpected roles, allowing each a place to display their range. But make no mistake, this is Driver's movie. What's Paper Tiger about? Set in 1986 New York City, Paper Tiger unfurls the story of a Jewish family from Queens that gets on the wrong side of the Russian mob. In a cozy home in Elmhurst, Irwin Pearl (Teller) raises his two sons, Benjamin (Roman Engel) and Scott (Gavin Goudey), with his dedicated housewife Linda (Johansson). Far from the cocky persona Teller forged through performances in The Spectacular Now, Whiplash , and the Divergent film series, the 39-year-old actor now oozes doofy dad energy. Teller's signature smirk is swapped for an aw-shucks smile, and a patronizing eyebrow raise that insists, "Father knows best." A pair of oversized eyeglasses completes the look; it's is such an evocative detail of the era that the title card reading "1986" might be deemed egregious. body: As the divide between older and younger generations continues to dictate everything from politics to entertainment to social media, one thing should be obvious: Baby Boomers, those born between 1948 and 1964, aren't ready to go quietly into retirement or hand the reins to today's youth. In fact, many of them are keeping things fresh by rekindling their romantic flames . According to Pew research , a massive 20 percent of Boomers have tried dating apps, and they spend just under 40 minutes a day trying their luck at the dating game. Don't expect to find the Baby Boomers on Tinder , though. For long-term dating, the Boomers are more likely to use age-appropriate dating services like OurTime or SeniorMatch, or larger, more general-purpose dating sites like eharmony, according to Axios . But there's an entire cohort of older daters who aren't focused on finding a long-term partner but still want to connect, and they're increasingly doing so on retro dating platforms such as AdultFriendFinder. body: If you like playing daily word games like Wordle , then Hurdle is a great game to add to your routine. There are five rounds to the game. The first round sees you trying to guess the word, with correct, misplaced, and incorrect letters shown in each guess. If you guess the correct answer, it'll take you to the next hurdle, providing the answer to the last hurdle as your first guess. This can give you several clues or none, depending on the words. For the final hurdle, every correct answer from previous hurdles is shown, with correct and misplaced letters clearly shown. An important note is that the number of times a letter is highlighted from previous guesses does necessarily indicate the number of times that letter appears in the final hurdle.
